beats.caption: Deon runs Moon Tees, a T-shirt company in his garage. His printer just broke, and orders keep coming.
beats.a11y: Deon at his workbench. His shirt printer puffs smoke and stops, and a stack of order boxes appears in front of the bench. Atlas blinks.

beats.caption: Let's say a new printer costs $600. Deon can sell pieces of Moon Tees, or borrow the money.
beats.a11y: The broken printer fades to a dashed outline: the printer Deon needs. Atlas blinks at the empty spot.

beats.caption: His friend Sriyan lends Moon Tees $300. Moon Tees will pay it back later, plus extra.
beats.a11y: Sriyan walks up the driveway to Deon's table with a gold coin. He hands it over, and Deon hands back a teal loan paper.

beats.caption: Then his friend Sid pays $300 for a piece of Moon Tees. Now he owns part of it.
beats.a11y: Sid walks up from the other side with a gold coin. He hands it to Deon, and Deon hands back a purple card: a piece of Moon Tees.

beats.caption: Deon buys the new printer. Sid's piece works like a stock, and Sriyan's loan works like a bond.
beats.a11y: Back in the garage, a new printer lands on the bench and glints. Sriyan holds his teal paper, Sid his purple card. Atlas does a happy hop.

toggles.title: Sriyan's loan
toggles.footer: Example deal. Many real bonds from companies and governments work this way.

states.caption: Sriyan lends Moon Tees money for 2 years. In return, Moon Tees makes him two promises.
states.a11y: Sriyan hands Deon a gold coin, his 300 dollar loan, and Deon hands back a teal loan paper.

states.caption: Promise 1: every six months, Moon Tees pays him the same extra for using his money. 4 payments, $60 in all.
states.a11y: Four small coins come from Deon one at a time and stack up on the ground beside Sriyan, 15 dollars each. Sriyan still holds his loan paper.

states.caption: Promise 2: on a set day 2 years from now, Moon Tees pays back all the money Sriyan lent.
states.a11y: Sriyan hands the loan paper back, and his gold coin comes back to him, landing on top of his four small coins.

states.caption: A great year! Someone might now pay Sid more for his piece. But it only turns into cash if he sells it.
states.a11y: Moon Tees on a busy night, string lights and a full rack of shirts. Sid's purple card glints, marked as worth 360 dollars.

states.caption: Moon Tees may also pay its owners some of what it earned, in cash. It can choose to, but it doesn't have to.
states.a11y: Deon slides a small gold coin, 20 dollars, onto the ground in front of Sid. Sid still holds his purple card.

states.caption: A slow year. Sid's piece is worth less now, and owners get no cash. Nobody promised Sid anything.
states.a11y: The rack is nearly empty and the lamp burns low. Sid's purple card is marked as worth 240 dollars.

toggles.title: If Moon Tees goes broke
toggles.footer: Example company and numbers. The order is real: lenders are paid before owners.

states.caption: Let's say sales stop. Moon Tees runs out of money and shuts down, so Deon sells the printer.
states.a11y: The garage door is down and the lamp is out. The printer on the table fades away, and a gold coin appears in Deon's hand.

states.caption: Lenders get paid first, so it all goes to Sriyan. He still gets back less than the $300 he lent.
states.a11y: The gold coin slides from Deon to the ground in front of Sriyan. Sid waits and gets nothing.

states.caption: Owners get whatever is left. Nothing is left, so Sid's piece is now worth nothing.
states.a11y: Sid's purple card fades to a dashed outline. Sriyan's coin lies at his feet, 200 dollars, and Sid gets 0 dollars.

toggles.title: Savings, bonds and stocks
toggles.footer: Sources: SEC (investor.gov) and NYU Stern, 1928 to 2025. The past is not a promise.

states.caption: Lesson 2 put these in order. Over long periods, insured savings have grown the least, but they don't drop.
states.a11y: On the bench, a small bank with the smallest up arrow and no down arrow. A loan paper and a purple card wait, dimmed. Atlas floats over the bank.

states.caption: Over long periods, bonds grew more than savings, less than stocks. Being paid first helps them lose less.
states.a11y: The loan paper lights up with medium up and down arrows, bigger than the bank's. Atlas floats over it.

states.caption: Over long periods, stocks have grown the most. But big US stocks lost money in about 1 of every 4 years.
states.a11y: The purple card lights up with the biggest up and down arrows. All three sit in a row, smallest arrows to biggest. Atlas floats over the card.
